title: verify_seal() swallows SymbolicGovernorViolation, losing original failure reason
description: Inside verify_seal() the inner try/except catches SymbolicGovernorViolation and returns False instead of re-raising. The require_cleared_seal decorator then raises a brand-new SymbolicGovernorViolation with a generic message, permanently discarding the original context (e.g. 'replay attack detected', 'TTL expired').
impact: Audit trails receive incorrect failure reasons. Forensic analysis of seal failures is unreliable. Any future code path that branches on the exception reason string may execute the wrong branch.
recommendation: Remove the inner SymbolicGovernorViolation catch inside verify_seal() and let it propagate. The require_cleared_seal decorator should not re-catch it.
dev_vs_prod: Affects both environments equally.

title: execute_trade() hardcodes side='buy', ignoring order.side entirely
description: The broker API payload at line 88 contains the string literal "side": "buy". The TradeOrder.side field is never read. Every trade — regardless of whether the order specifies 'sell' — is submitted to Alpaca as a buy.
impact: All sell orders silently become buy orders. A risk-reduction sell instruction becomes a position-increasing buy, causing runaway long exposure and potential regulatory violations (MiFID II best-execution, FINRA suitability).
recommendation: Replace the hardcoded string with "side": order.side (or order.side.value if side is an Enum). Add an integration test asserting the broker payload contains side=sell for sell orders.
dev_vs_prod: Equally critical in both environments.

title: pre_check() treats CBF exceptions as SAFE (fail-open), contradicting the system's fail-closed posture
description: In pre_check() the CBF check is wrapped in a bare try/except. When the CBF raises any exception (Redis unavailable, WatchError, etc.) the code logs a warning and continues, treating the action as safe. Every other safety gate (OPA, routing seal, fiscal guard) fails closed.
impact: If Redis is unavailable, the Control Barrier Function is silently bypassed. An attacker who can cause Redis to be unreachable can bypass the CBF and execute trades that violate cash-balance invariants.
recommendation: Re-raise the exception (or raise GovernanceError) unless CBF_FAIL_OPEN=true is explicitly set. The existing CBF_FAIL_OPEN env-var check in _run_checks() already handles the intentional fail-open case.
dev_vs_prod: More dangerous in production where Redis failures are real infrastructure events.

title: Default GOVERNANCE_SALT is a well-known string; assert_custom_salt_in_production() is never called automatically
description: The module-level default _SALT = os.environ.get('GOVERNANCE_SALT', 'default-governance-salt-change-in-production') means any deployment that omits GOVERNANCE_SALT uses a publicly known HMAC key. assert_custom_salt_in_production() exists but is only called if the operator explicitly invokes it — it is not called during module import, lifespan startup, or any automatic path.
impact: An attacker who knows the default salt (it is in the source code) can forge valid routing seals for any action/params combination, bypassing the No-Direct-Bind invariant entirely.
recommendation: Call assert_custom_salt_in_production() unconditionally in the hybrid_server.py lifespan function alongside assert_kms_active_in_production(). Alternatively raise at module import time if CAGE_ENV=production and the salt is the default value.
dev_vs_prod: Critical in production. Weak default is acceptable in dev but should be documented.

category: Logic Bug — State Corruption on Validation Failure
title: execute_trade_action() updates CBF state before validating TradeOrder, leaving state dirty on Pydantic error
description: The call to symbolic_governor.safety_filter.update_state(amount) occurs before TradeOrder(**params) is constructed. If TradeOrder construction raises a ValidationError (invalid symbol, negative amount, etc.), the CBF cash-balance has already been decremented but no trade was executed. The except block only rolls back on execute_trade() exceptions, not on TradeOrder construction failures.
impact: Each failed TradeOrder construction permanently reduces the CBF's tracked cash balance without a corresponding trade. Over time this causes the CBF to believe less cash is available than actually exists, eventually blocking all legitimate trades with false-positive governance refusals.
recommendation: Move update_state() to after successful TradeOrder construction, or wrap the entire block (TradeOrder construction + execute_trade) in a single try/except with rollback_state() in the except clause.
dev_vs_prod: Affects both environments; more likely to accumulate in production under load.

title: execute_trade_action() has no confidence parameter; defaults to 0.0, always failing the confidence gate
description: The MCP tool function execute_trade_action() does not declare a confidence parameter in its signature. The governance params dict passed to symbolic_governor.govern() therefore contains confidence=0.0. The GovernanceThresholds.min_trade_confidence is 0.7 by default. Every trade submitted through the MCP tool fails the confidence check.
impact: The MCP tool path is permanently broken for any deployment with confidence thresholds enabled. All trades via the MCP interface are refused at the confidence gate, making the tool non-functional for its primary purpose.
recommendation: Add confidence: float = 0.0 to the execute_trade_action() signature and pass it through to the governance params. Document that callers must supply a real confidence value.
dev_vs_prod: Affects both environments equally.

title: stamp_iso_control() is a complete no-op for EU_ECB and APAC_MAS regions
description: Lines 104-110 check `if region != 'US_FED': return` before writing any OTel span attributes. The function name and docstring imply universal ISO 42001 evidence stamping, but EU_ECB and APAC_MAS deployments receive zero compliance evidence on any governance span. The function silently returns without logging a warning.
impact: ISO 42001 Clause 6.1 audit evidence is absent for all non-US_FED deployments. Lula validation assertions that check for ISO control stamps on spans will fail or produce false-positive passes. EU_ECB and APAC_MAS compliance postures are materially weaker than documented.
recommendation: Remove the region guard or make it additive: stamp universal ISO 42001 attributes for all regions, then add region-specific attributes (NIST control IDs for US_FED, EU AI Act articles for EU_ECB, MAS FEAT for APAC_MAS) conditionally.
dev_vs_prod: Affects all non-US_FED production deployments.

category: Security — Synthetic Data in Production Safety Check
title: causal_safety_check() falls back to generate_mock_telemetry() when no telemetry is provided
description: When current_telemetry is None (the default), causal_safety_check() calls generate_mock_telemetry() to produce synthetic market data and runs the DoWhy placebo refutation against it. The mock data uses np.random.seed(42) — a fixed, deterministic seed — so the causal check always produces the same result for the same action_type/market_regime combination regardless of actual market conditions.
impact: In production, if the LangfuseTelemetryProvider fails to fetch data, the causal gate silently runs against synthetic data. The fixed seed makes the result predictable and potentially gameable by an attacker who knows the seed.
recommendation: When current_telemetry is None in a production context (CAGE_ENV=production), raise a GovernanceError rather than falling back to mock data. Reserve the mock fallback for dev/test environments only, gated on CAGE_ENV.
dev_vs_prod: Critical in production. Mock fallback is intentional and acceptable in dev.

title: Causal cache key omits trade amount; different amounts share the same cached result
description: The cache key is constructed as `f'causal:{action_type}:{market_regime}'`. The trade amount is not included. A $100 trade and a $10,000,000 trade with the same action_type and market_regime share the same cached causal safety result.
impact: A small, safe trade can pre-warm the cache with a SAFE result, after which arbitrarily large trades of the same type bypass the causal check for the entire cache TTL. This is a cache-poisoning vector that undermines the causal gatekeeper's financial safety guarantees.
recommendation: Include a bucketed representation of the amount in the cache key (e.g. order-of-magnitude bucket: `amount_bucket = int(math.log10(max(amount, 1)))`). Alternatively include the exact amount if cache hit rates are acceptable.
dev_vs_prod: More dangerous in production where the cache TTL is meaningful and multiple agents share the Redis instance.

title: _sign_record() silently falls back to HMAC stub when KMS signing fails
description: In _sign_record(), lines 416-435, if KMSGovernanceSigner raises any exception during signing, the code catches it, logs a warning, and falls back to a stub HMAC signature using hmac.new(b'stub-key', ...). The audit record is persisted with a weak, predictable signature. No alert is raised, no metric is incremented, and the record's signature field does not indicate the downgrade.
impact: Audit records that should be KMS-signed (for non-repudiation and tamper evidence) are silently signed with a known stub key. An attacker who can cause KMS to be temporarily unavailable can cause all subsequent audit records to be weakly signed, undermining the WORM ledger's integrity guarantees.
recommendation: In production (CAGE_ENV=production), re-raise the KMS exception rather than falling back. In dev, set a distinct signature_method field in the record (e.g. 'HMAC_STUB_DEV') so consumers can distinguish it from a real KMS signature.
dev_vs_prod: Critical in production. Stub fallback is acceptable in dev for offline testing.

category: Logic Bug — Token Quota Not Rolled Back on NeMo Block
title: Token quota incremented before NeMo check; NeMo blocks (non-exception) do not trigger rollback
description: In chat_completions(), the token quota is checked and incremented via check_and_increment() before the NeMo guardrails check. If NeMo returns a blocked response (not an exception — it returns a structured block result), the code path falls through to _create_blocked_response() without calling rollback_step(). Only the except block triggers rollback.
impact: Every NeMo-blocked request permanently consumes token quota. Under a prompt-injection attack (which NeMo is designed to catch), the attacker can exhaust the victim agent's token quota by sending many blocked requests, causing a denial-of-service against legitimate governance operations.
recommendation: After the NeMo check, if the result indicates a block (not an exception), explicitly call `await quota_proxy.rollback_step(agent_id, estimated_tokens, 1)` before returning the blocked response.
dev_vs_prod: More impactful in production where quota limits are enforced.

title: get_governance_signer() singleton is not thread-safe; concurrent calls can create multiple KMSGovernanceSigner instances
description: get_governance_signer() checks `if _signer is None` and then assigns `_signer = KMSGovernanceSigner.from_env()` without any lock. Under concurrent FastAPI request handling, two coroutines can both observe `_signer is None` simultaneously and both call from_env(), resulting in two KMS client initializations and two distinct signer objects.
impact: KMS client connections are leaked on startup under concurrent load. If KMS initialization is rate-limited, concurrent initialization can exhaust KMS API quotas or cause initialization failures.
recommendation: Use asyncio.Lock (for async contexts) or threading.Lock (for sync contexts) around the singleton initialization, or use a module-level lock with double-checked locking.
dev_vs_prod: More likely to manifest in production under concurrent request load.

title: ControlRegistry.reconfigure() has a TOCTOU race: clears _instance outside the lock then re-creates it
description: reconfigure() first acquires the lock to clear cls._instance = None, then releases the lock, then calls ControlRegistry() which re-acquires the lock to create a new instance. Between the clear and the re-creation, another thread calling ControlRegistry() will see _instance is None and create its own instance with the old region.
impact: During a normative provider baseline refresh, concurrent governance checks may briefly use a ControlRegistry with the wrong region profile. In a multi-region deployment this could cause US_FED controls to be evaluated against EU_ECB mappings.
recommendation: Hold the lock for the entire reconfigure() operation: clear _instance and create the new one within a single lock acquisition. Use threading.RLock since ControlRegistry.__new__() also acquires the lock.
dev_vs_prod: Only manifests under concurrent load; more likely in production.

title: WatchError detected via class name string matching instead of catching the actual exception type
description: In update_state() and rollback_state(), WatchError from redis.asyncio is caught via `except Exception as exc: if 'WatchError' in type(exc).__name__`. This string-matching approach fails if the redis library renames the exception, if a different exception with 'WatchError' in its name is raised, or if the exception is wrapped in another type.
impact: A genuine WatchError (concurrent modification of the cash-balance key) may not be caught and re-raised as TransactionAbortedError, instead propagating as a generic Exception. Callers that retry on TransactionAbortedError will not retry, leaving the CBF state inconsistent.
recommendation: Import redis.asyncio at the top of cbf.py and catch redis.asyncio.WatchError directly. The redis_client.py module already handles WatchError correctly using the actual exception type.
dev_vs_prod: Affects both environments; more likely to cause issues under concurrent load in production.

title: asyncio.create_task() in enforce_fria_boundary() stores no reference; task can be garbage-collected mid-execution
description: At line 388, asyncio.create_task(_async_attestation(...)) is called without storing the returned Task object. Python's asyncio documentation explicitly warns that tasks not referenced by the caller can be garbage-collected mid-execution. The attestation coroutine may be silently cancelled before it completes.
impact: FRIA attestation evidence may not be submitted to the normative provider. ISO 42001 Annex A evidence chains will have gaps. In a compliance audit, missing attestation records could constitute a control failure.
recommendation: Store the task in a module-level set and add a done callback to remove it: `_background_tasks = set(); t = asyncio.create_task(...); _background_tasks.add(t); t.add_done_callback(_background_tasks.discard)`.
dev_vs_prod: Affects both environments; GC timing is non-deterministic and harder to reproduce in dev.

title: StubNormativeProvider.validate_fria() always returns admitted=True regardless of payload
description: The StubNormativeProvider (development-only provider) implements validate_fria() as a no-op that always returns ValidationResult(admitted=True, reason='stub'). If this provider is accidentally used in production (NORMATIVE_PROVIDER env var unset or set to 'stub'), all FRIA boundary checks pass unconditionally.
impact: All FRIA enforcement is bypassed. Transactions that should be deferred to the DeferQueue (low-confidence, high-risk) are admitted without review, undermining the adaptive FRIA enforcement mechanism entirely.
recommendation: Add a production guard: if CAGE_ENV=production and the resolved provider is StubNormativeProvider, raise RuntimeError at startup. Log a prominent WARNING when StubNormativeProvider is used in any environment.
dev_vs_prod: Only dangerous in production; intentional in dev.

category: Concurrency — Race Condition in Aho-Corasick Automaton Build
title: _AC_AUTOMATON and _AC_BUILT module globals are not thread-safe; concurrent requests can double-build the automaton
description: The module-level globals _AC_AUTOMATON and _AC_BUILT are checked and set in _build_automaton() without any lock. Under concurrent FastAPI request handling, two coroutines can both observe _AC_BUILT=False simultaneously and both call _build_automaton(), resulting in two automaton builds and a race on the assignment to _AC_AUTOMATON.
impact: The automaton may be partially constructed when a concurrent request reads it, causing incorrect keyword scan results (false negatives). A prompt-injection keyword could pass the Tier-1 filter because the automaton was read in an inconsistent state.
recommendation: Use threading.Lock around the _build_automaton() call and the _AC_BUILT check, or initialize the automaton at module import time (eagerly) rather than lazily.
dev_vs_prod: Only manifests under concurrent load; more likely in production.

title: _load_scripts() is not atomic; concurrent calls load Lua scripts multiple times
description: The _load_scripts() method checks `if self._scripts_loaded` and then sets it to True after loading, without any lock. Multiple concurrent coroutines can all observe _scripts_loaded=False and all call Redis SCRIPT LOAD simultaneously.
impact: Under high concurrency at startup, multiple SCRIPT LOAD calls are issued. If Redis is rate-limiting connections (e.g. Cloud Memorystore connection limits), this can cause initialization failures that block all quota checks.
recommendation: Use asyncio.Lock to serialize _load_scripts() calls: `async with self._load_lock: if not self._scripts_loaded: ...`.
dev_vs_prod: More likely to manifest in production under concurrent startup load.

title: _is_async_client() uses module name string matching to detect async Redis clients
description: _is_async_client() checks 'asyncio' in type(self._redis).__module__ or 'aioredis' in type(self._redis).__module__. This heuristic fails for any future async Redis client library that doesn't include those strings in its module path, and for mock objects in tests.
impact: If _is_async_client() returns False for an actual async client, the sync code path (_sync_atomic_increment) is called from an async context, blocking the event loop. This causes latency spikes and can deadlock the entire gateway under load.
recommendation: Use isinstance(self._redis, redis.asyncio.Redis) for a type-safe check, or require callers to pass an explicit is_async: bool flag at construction time.
dev_vs_prod: Affects both environments; more likely to cause issues when the Redis client library is updated.

category: Reliability — asyncio Primitive Created Before Event Loop
title: _explain_queue asyncio.Queue created at module import time, before the event loop exists
description: Line 59 creates `_explain_queue: asyncio.Queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=1000)` at module level. In Python 3.10+, creating asyncio primitives before the event loop is running is deprecated and raises DeprecationWarning. In Python 3.12+, it raises RuntimeError. The same issue exists in consensus.py with _AUDIT_QUEUE.
impact: On Python 3.12+, importing policy.py raises RuntimeError, preventing the gateway from starting. On Python 3.10-3.11, it works but emits deprecation warnings that may be treated as errors in CI.
recommendation: Initialize the queue lazily inside start_explain_worker() or use a module-level variable initialized to None and set it in the worker startup function.
dev_vs_prod: Affects both environments on Python 3.12+. Python version pinning in the Dockerfile may mask this in production.

title: evaluate_policy() returns raw OPA result when uncached but str(result) when cached
description: In evaluate_policy(), the cache write stores `decision_str = str(result)` and the cache read returns the string. However, the uncached path returns `result` directly (which may be a dict, list, or other type depending on OPA's response). Callers in symbolic_governor.py that do string comparisons will work for cached responses but may fail for uncached responses if OPA returns a dict.
impact: Non-deterministic behavior depending on cache state. A cold-cache request may behave differently from a warm-cache request for the same input. This is particularly dangerous for governance decisions where consistency is critical.
recommendation: Normalize the return value: always return str(result) from evaluate_policy(), or always return the parsed dict. Update all callers to use the normalized type.
dev_vs_prod: More likely to manifest in production where cache hit rates vary.

title: _pending_payload instance variable is not thread-safe under concurrent requests
description: SymbolicGovernor stores self._pending_payload as an instance variable set during _run_checks() and read in govern(). If the SymbolicGovernor singleton handles concurrent requests (which it does), two concurrent govern() calls will overwrite each other's _pending_payload. The second call's payload will be used for the first call's routing seal generation.
impact: Under concurrent load, the routing seal for request A may be generated using the params from request B. This causes seal verification failures for request A and potentially allows request B's params to bypass seal verification.
recommendation: Use a local variable instead of an instance variable: pass the payload through the call chain as a parameter rather than storing it on self. Alternatively, use contextvars.ContextVar to make it per-coroutine.
dev_vs_prod: Only manifests under concurrent load; more likely in production.

category: Logic Bug — Parameter Mismatch in Causal Check
title: symbolic_governor passes params wrapped in a dict but causal_safety_check expects amount at top level
description: In symbolic_governor.py, the causal check is called with causal_safety_check({'params': params, 'telemetry': telemetry_data}). However, causal_safety_check() accesses params.get('amount', 0) at the top level of its input dict. The actual amount is at params['params']['amount'], not params['amount']. This means amount is always 0 for the causal check.
impact: The causal safety check always uses amount=0 regardless of the actual trade size. The statistical kernel and placebo refutation run against a zero-amount trade, making the causal gate ineffective for large trades.
recommendation: Either flatten the params dict before passing to causal_safety_check(), or update causal_safety_check() to accept the nested structure. Add a unit test that verifies the amount is correctly propagated.
dev_vs_prod: Affects both environments equally.

title: API key regex pattern misses OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS, and GCP service account key formats
description: The _PII_PATTERNS list covers pk-lf-, sk-lf-, hf_, and Bearer prefixes but not: OpenAI keys (sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{48}), Anthropic keys (sk-ant-...), GCP service account JSON (private_key fields), AWS access keys (AKIA[A-Z0-9]{16}), or generic JWT tokens (eyJ...).
impact: Credentials in these formats pass through the PII sanitizer and may be persisted to the WORM ledger or Langfuse telemetry, violating ISO 42001 Annex A.6 data minimization requirements and potentially exposing live credentials in audit logs.
recommendation: Add patterns for OpenAI (sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}), Anthropic (sk-ant-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{90,}), AWS (AKIA[A-Z0-9]{16}), and JWT (eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]+). Consider using a dedicated secrets-detection library (e.g. detect-secrets).
dev_vs_prod: Affects both environments; more impactful in production where real credentials are in use.

title: Production guard uses ENVIRONMENT env var while the rest of the codebase uses CAGE_ENV
description: The production guard at line 137 checks os.getenv('ENVIRONMENT') == 'production'. All other production guards in the codebase (assert_kms_active_in_production, assert_custom_salt_in_production, etc.) check CAGE_ENV. Additionally, the guard uses an assert statement which can be disabled with Python's -O (optimize) flag.
impact: If CAGE_ENV=production but ENVIRONMENT is unset, the production guard silently passes, skipping KMS and salt validation. The assert statement can be disabled entirely with python -O, bypassing the guard in optimized deployments.
recommendation: Standardize on CAGE_ENV throughout. Replace the assert with an explicit if/raise block: `if os.getenv('CAGE_ENV') == 'production': assert_custom_salt_in_production(); assert_kms_active_in_production()`.
dev_vs_prod: Only affects production deployments where ENVIRONMENT is not set.

title: logger.error() used to log a successful OSCAL receipt emission
description: At line 398, after successfully emitting an OSCAL compliance receipt, the code calls logger.error('OSCAL receipt emitted', ...). This is a successful operation logged at ERROR level, which will trigger alerts and noise in production monitoring systems.
impact: Every successful governance refusal (which triggers OSCAL receipt emission) generates a spurious ERROR log entry. This desensitizes operators to ERROR-level alerts and makes it harder to identify real errors in log aggregation systems.
recommendation: Change logger.error() to logger.info() for the successful OSCAL receipt emission. Reserve ERROR level for actual failures (e.g. the except block below it).
dev_vs_prod: Affects both environments; more impactful in production where log-based alerting is active.

category: Compatibility — Deprecated asyncio API in Generated Code
title: Generated LangGraph code uses asyncio.get_event_loop().run_until_complete(), deprecated in Python 3.10+
description: The generate_langgraph() function emits code that calls asyncio.get_event_loop().run_until_complete(). In Python 3.10+, get_event_loop() is deprecated when there is no running event loop. In Python 3.12+, it raises DeprecationWarning. If the generated code is called from within an async context (e.g. inside a FastAPI handler), run_until_complete() raises RuntimeError: 'This event loop is already running'.
impact: Generated saga compensation nodes cannot be executed from within the async gateway. Any STPA-generated LangGraph saga that is triggered during a governance check will raise RuntimeError, causing the saga to fail silently or crash the handler.
recommendation: Replace asyncio.get_event_loop().run_until_complete(coro) with asyncio.run(coro) in generated code for top-level scripts, or use await coro directly for async contexts. Add a template parameter to generate_langgraph() to select the appropriate pattern.
dev_vs_prod: Affects both environments on Python 3.10+.

title: VLLM_API_KEY falls back to the string 'EMPTY', potentially allowing unauthenticated vLLM access
description: Line 31 sets api_key=Config.VLLM_API_KEY or 'EMPTY'. The string 'EMPTY' is the vLLM server's default accepted key when authentication is disabled. If VLLM_API_KEY is not set in the environment, the gateway connects to vLLM with the well-known 'EMPTY' key, which may be accepted by a misconfigured vLLM instance.
impact: If the vLLM server is deployed with default authentication settings (accepting 'EMPTY'), any client that knows this default can bypass authentication. In a shared cluster, other pods could impersonate the gateway to the vLLM backend.
recommendation: Require VLLM_API_KEY to be set in production: raise ValueError at startup if CAGE_ENV=production and VLLM_API_KEY is unset. Do not fall back to 'EMPTY' silently.
dev_vs_prod: Acceptable in dev where vLLM runs locally. Critical risk in production if vLLM accepts 'EMPTY'.

title: ssl_cert_reqs=ssl.CERT_NONE disables certificate validation for Redis TLS connections in all environments
description: Both _AsyncRedisClient and _SyncRedisClient set ssl_cert_reqs=ssl.CERT_NONE when TLS is enabled. The comment says 'allow self-signed certs in dev/GKE'. This means certificate validation is disabled even in production GKE deployments using Cloud Memorystore, where a valid CA-signed certificate is available.
impact: Without certificate validation, the Redis connection is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. An attacker with network access between the gateway pod and Cloud Memorystore could intercept or modify Redis traffic, including CBF cash-balance values and OPA decision cache entries.
recommendation: In production (CAGE_ENV=production or REDIS_TLS=true without REDIS_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY=true), set ssl_cert_reqs=ssl.CERT_REQUIRED and provide the CA certificate path via REDIS_CA_CERT env var. Reserve CERT_NONE for dev environments only.
dev_vs_prod: Low risk in dev (self-signed certs). Medium-to-high risk in production where MITM is a realistic threat.

category: Performance — N+1 Redis Calls in list_pending()
title: list_pending() issues one HGET per token instead of using a pipeline or HMGET
description: list_pending() first calls ZRANGEBYSCORE to get all pending token IDs, then issues a separate HGET call for each token ID in a loop. For N pending tokens, this results in N+1 Redis round-trips. Under high deferral load (many low-confidence transactions parked), this can cause significant latency.
impact: Under load, list_pending() can take O(N) Redis round-trips. If called frequently (e.g. by a monitoring endpoint or the replay evaluator), this can saturate the Redis connection pool and cause latency spikes across all governance operations that share the same Redis instance.
recommendation: Use a Redis pipeline to batch the HGET calls: `async with redis.pipeline() as pipe: [pipe.hget(hash_key, tid) for tid in token_ids]; results = await pipe.execute()`. Alternatively use HMGET if all tokens share the same hash key.
dev_vs_prod: Low impact in dev with few deferred tokens. Significant in production under sustained low-confidence traffic.
